docs.t: How to connect your business apps: Why the same job gets typed into three systems
docs.a: Picture a Monday morning at a small homewares shop. An online order came in overnight. Someone copies it into the packing spreadsheet, then creates the customer in Xero, then types the sale in again so the books match. Nobody planned it that way. Most small businesses didn't choose their software all at once. The accounting software came first, then an online store, then a booking app, then a spreadsheet someone set up to track jobs. Each tool does its own job well. The trouble is that none of them knows what the others are doing. So people fill the gaps. A job is booked by email and someone creates the customer in Xero. A supplier invoice lands in Outlook and someone keys it into the accounting software. Each step only takes a little while, but they happen all day. And every retype is a chance for a typo, a missed order or an invoice that never goes out. You're not alone. On our home page we describe this as "no more retyping the same job into three systems." Copying details between two systems turns up in almost every industry.

docs.t: How to connect your business apps: How app connections work: when this, do that
docs.a: Almost every connection between two apps follows the same simple pattern: when this happens here, do that over there. There are three parts to it. Triggers A trigger is the event that starts things off. A new order in your online store, a form submitted on your website, or an email arriving with an attachment. It could also be a quote marked as accepted, or a new row added to a spreadsheet. Actions An action is what happens as a result. Create an invoice, add a customer, send a message, update a row or save a file to a folder. One trigger can lead to several actions in a row. Matching records This is the part that takes the most care. When an order arrives, the connection has to decide whether this customer already exists in your accounting software or needs to be created. It usually matches on something unique, like an email address or customer number. Get matching wrong and you end up with three versions of the same customer, which is worse than retyping. Apps talk through doors called APIs. An API is a way for one app to let another app read or write information, with your permission. You'll hear the word a lot. All you really need to know is that most modern business software has one, and that's what makes connections possible.

docs.t: How to connect your business apps: Map your data flow before you connect anything
docs.a: Before connecting anything, draw how information moves through your business today. A whiteboard or a sheet of paper is fine. List your apps. Everything that holds business information, including spreadsheets, shared inboxes and paper forms. Follow one job from start to finish. Where does the first enquiry arrive? Where is it booked, quoted, delivered, invoiced and paid? Mark every retype. Each time a person copies information from one place to another, draw an arrow. These arrows are your candidates for connection. Note who does each step. The person doing the retyping usually knows exactly where it goes wrong. Pick the busiest arrow. Start with the copy that happens most often or causes the most mistakes. Your map is also handy for deciding what to automate first , because it shows where the effort really goes.

docs.t: How to connect your business apps: Useful app connections for NZ small businesses
docs.a: Here are common connections between tools many New Zealand businesses already use. Each one swaps a manual copy for an automatic one. The tools we connect are Microsoft 365, Google Workspace and Xero. Where another system is involved, such as an online store or point-of-sale, we work from the emails or Excel and Google Sheets exports it already produces, rather than connecting to it directly. When this happens This happens automatically An order confirmation email arrives from your online store A packing row is added to Google Sheets, and the sale is recorded in Xero A supplier invoice arrives in Gmail or Outlook The details go into Xero as a draft bill for checking A customer accepts a quote A draft invoice is created in Xero with the approved line items A website enquiry form is submitted The contact is added to your customer list in Excel or Google Sheets and the right person is alerted by email or in Teams Your point-of-sale system emails its end-of-day sales report A summary is added to an Excel or Google Sheets file and sent to the owner's phone Notice the word "draft" in a couple of those rows. A person still checks the bill or invoice before it's final. Want to see one of these end to end? Our guide to automating quotes and invoices walks through it. And the weekly business numbers guide shows how connected apps can feed a single summary.

docs.t: How to connect your business apps: Keep one source of truth for your data
docs.a: When apps are connected, the same information can appear in several places. That's fine, as long as everyone knows which app is in charge of it. This is called the source of truth. For example, you might decide that: Customer contact details live in your customer list, such as an Excel or Google Sheets file. Invoices and payments live in your accounting software. Stock levels live in your point-of-sale or online store. Bookings live in your booking app. The rule is simple: change information only in its source of truth, and let the connections carry the change everywhere else. Say someone updates a customer's phone number in the accounting software instead. The next sync may overwrite it, or you end up with two numbers and no idea which is right. Write it down. A one-page list of "this information lives here" saves a lot of confusion, especially for new staff.

docs.t: How to connect your business apps: When a connection fails: errors and alerts
docs.a: Every connection will fail sometimes. An app goes down for maintenance, a password changes, someone renames a column in a spreadsheet, or an order arrives with a missing email address. What matters is what happens next. A good alert tells the right person what's stuck and why: Heads-up: last night's order #2187 couldn't be added to Xero because it has no email address. It's been saved and is waiting. Add the email and it'll go through on the next retry. Behind that message sit four habits every connection needs: Catch the failure. The connection should notice it didn't work, rather than carry on as if it did. Keep the information. Whatever failed should be held so it can be retried, not lost. Alert a named person. Decide who gets told, how (email, text or a message) and how quickly. "Someone will notice" isn't a plan. Retry and confirm. Once fixed, the stuck items should go through, and someone should check they arrived. Whoever builds your connections, ask how failures will be reported, who will be told and who will fix them. Then get the answer written into the scope. Be careful with connections that delete or overwrite. A mistake that creates a duplicate is easy to tidy up. A mistake that deletes records or overwrites good data is much harder to undo. Test these on sample data first.

docs.t: How to connect your business apps: Access, security and personal information
docs.a: Connecting apps means giving one app permission to read or write information in another. Keep that permission as narrow as you can. Only pass across the fields the other app needs. Use a business account rather than someone's personal login. Review access when staff leave. Own every login involved, so you're never locked out of your own systems. If the information includes customer or staff details, the Privacy Act 2020 applies. Our guide to the Privacy Act 2020 and automation covers what to check.

docs.t: How to connect your business apps: When a spreadsheet is fine, and when to connect your apps
docs.a: Not every gap needs a connection. A shared Google Sheets or Excel file is often the right tool when volumes are small, one or two people use it, and the information doesn't need to reach anywhere else. Spreadsheets are cheap, flexible and everyone understands them. It's time to connect when you notice: The same details are typed into the spreadsheet and another app every week. Mistakes in copying are costing you money or customers. Several people edit the sheet at once and things get overwritten. You spend more than a few hours a week keeping it up to date. Even then, the spreadsheet can stay. Often the best first step is simply to fill it automatically, so it keeps doing its job without anyone typing into it. That's a small, low-risk change, and a good way to see what connected apps can do for your business.

docs.t: Your business numbers, every week
docs.a: Most owners know roughly how the business is going, but the real figures are scattered across several apps. A short weekly summary puts the business numbers that matter in one place, so you can spot a problem while it's still small. Track a handful of numbers that lead to a decision: sales, unpaid invoices, cash, jobs, hours and stock. Every number should come straight from the system that already holds it, not from someone retyping it. Start with a Monday summary on your phone. Add a live dashboard only when you check the numbers during the week. Keep it to one screen, and decide who sees what before you build it. If a number never changes what you do, take it off.
docs.x: Your business numbers, every week Digital tools What to track, where the numbers come from, and how to get them on your phone every Monday.

docs.t: Do I need new software to get a weekly numbers summary?
docs.q: Do I need new software to get a weekly numbers summary?
docs.a: Usually not. The figures already live in Xero, your spreadsheets, and the reports your point of sale or booking system produces. A summary reads from Xero and from Excel or Google Sheets on a schedule, works from any export or emailed report your point of sale or booking system already produces, and puts the results in one message or screen.

docs.t: What is the difference between a weekly summary and a live dashboard?
docs.q: What is the difference between a weekly summary and a live dashboard?
docs.a: A weekly summary is a short message, often sent on Monday morning, that shows last week's numbers. A live dashboard is a screen you can open at any time that updates itself as new sales, jobs or payments come in. Many small businesses only need the summary.

docs.t: Can my staff see the dashboard without seeing the financials?
docs.q: Can my staff see the dashboard without seeing the financials?
docs.a: Yes. A well set up dashboard can show different views to different people, so a team leader might see jobs and hours while only the owner sees cash and unpaid invoices.

docs.t: How accurate will the numbers be?
docs.q: How accurate will the numbers be?
docs.a: They are only as accurate as the systems they come from. If invoices are entered late or stock counts are out of date, the summary will reflect that, which is often useful in itself because it shows where the records need tidying.

docs.t: Your business numbers, every week: Why a weekly look at your numbers beats a Sunday-night guess
docs.a: Picture Sunday night on the couch. Someone asks how the week went, and you say "pretty good, I think". It felt busy. The phone rang a lot. But you couldn't put a figure on it if you tried. That's not a criticism. Ask many owners how last week went and you'll get a feeling rather than a figure, because the figures are spread all over the place: your accounting software, your point of sale or booking system, a timesheet app, and a spreadsheet someone updates when they remember. Pulling them together takes time you don't have. So it happens at the end of the month, or when the accountant asks. The trouble is that problems grow quietly. An invoice that's a little overdue is a phone call. Leave it for months and it can become a write-off conversation. A short, regular look at the right numbers lets you act while the fix is still easy.

docs.t: Your business numbers, every week: The handful of numbers that usually matter
docs.a: You don't need dozens of measures. A handful is usually enough, as long as each one leads to a decision. Here's a starting list, with where each number usually comes from. Number What it tells you Where it usually comes from Sales How busy last week was, compared with the week before and the same week last year Point of sale, online shop or accounting software Unpaid invoices Who owes you, how much, and how overdue Accounting software such as Xero Cash What's actually in the bank, and what's due out this week Bank feed in your accounting software Jobs Jobs booked, in progress, finished and not yet invoiced Job management app, booking system or a shared spreadsheet Hours Staff hours worked against what was rostered or quoted Timesheet or rostering app, or payroll Stock Items running low, and stock that isn't moving Point of sale or inventory system, through an export to Excel or Google Sheets or an emailed report Pick the ones that fit your business. A café cares about stock and hours. A consultant may have no stock at all and care far more about jobs not yet invoiced. The test for every number. If it went up or down sharply, would you do something different this week? If the honest answer is no, it doesn't belong on the summary.

docs.t: Your business numbers, every week: Get every number straight from the source
docs.a: A summary is only useful if you trust it. And you'll only trust it if nobody is retyping figures into it. So the rule is simple: each number should be read automatically from the system that already holds it. No copying from one screen to another on a Friday afternoon. In practice, that means connecting your tools so they hand information to each other. Xero, Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace allow this through an API, which is a secure doorway one program uses to ask another for data. For other systems, such as a point of sale or booking system, we don't connect directly. Instead, an exported file, an emailed report or a shared Google Sheets or Excel file acts as the go-between. Our guide to connecting your business apps explains how these connections work and what to check first. Two things to sort out before you build anything: Agree what each number means. Does "sales" include or exclude GST? Is a job "finished" when the work is done, or when it's signed off? Write the definitions down once and stick to them. Find the gaps. If invoices are only entered at the end of the month, a weekly unpaid-invoices figure will be out of date for most of the month. Sometimes the first improvement is a small process change, not a dashboard.

docs.t: Your business numbers, every week: A Monday summary or a live dashboard?
docs.a: There are two common ways to see your numbers, and they suit different owners. The weekly summary A short message lands on your phone or in your inbox every Monday morning, before the week gets busy. Nobody has to remember to send it. It might look something like this: Your week at a glance (example only, figures made up) Sales: $10,000, up on the week before Overdue invoices over your set amount: 2, with names Cash on hand: $20,000 Jobs finished, not yet invoiced: 3 Hours worked: 100 against 90 rostered Low stock: 2 items below reorder point That's last week's sales, overdue invoices over a set amount, cash on hand, jobs waiting to be invoiced, hours worked and anything low in stock. It's quick to read over a coffee. For many small businesses this is the right place to start. It builds the habit of looking, and it's quick to set up because it only needs to read the numbers once a week. The live dashboard A dashboard is a single screen that updates itself as new sales, payments and jobs come in. You open it whenever you want, on your phone or a laptop. It suits businesses where things change during the day, such as a busy shop watching sales by hour, or a transport business watching deliveries completed. A good rule of thumb. If you find yourself wanting to check the Monday numbers on a Wednesday, it's time for a live view. Our websites, portals and dashboards service covers how we build these around the tools you already have.

docs.t: Your business numbers, every week: Keep your dashboard to one screen
docs.a: A common mistake is adding everything. Every extra chart makes the important numbers harder to see. Aim for something you can read on a phone without scrolling much. Put the decision numbers at the top. Cash, overdue invoices and anything that needs action today. Show a comparison. A number on its own means little. Show it next to last week, or the same week last year, so you can see the direction. Flag only what needs attention. Highlight, for example, an invoice that's more than 30 days overdue, or stock below its reorder point, and leave everything else plain. Link to the detail. The summary should tell you where to look, not try to show every line. A tap through to the accounting software or the job list is enough. Review it after a month. Remove anything nobody looked at, and add the one number you kept asking about.

docs.t: Your business numbers, every week: Who sees which numbers
docs.a: Not everyone needs every number, and some numbers should stay private. Decide this up front, because it shapes how the summary is built. The owner usually sees everything, including cash and who owes what. A manager or team leader may see jobs, hours and stock, but not bank balances. Your bookkeeper or accountant may only need the unpaid invoices and a monthly view. Staff might see a team figure, such as jobs completed this week, without any financial detail. Names are personal information. Unpaid invoices and timesheets often include customer and staff names. Keep access to the people who need it, and turn on two-factor authentication for anything that shows financial or personal details. Our guide to the Privacy Act 2020 and automation covers what else to check.

docs.t: Your business numbers, every week: What a weekly numbers report looks like by industry
docs.a: Here's what a Monday summary might hold for different kinds of business. Treat these as starting points, not templates. Café or takeaway Hospitality Sales by day, staff hours against the roster, supplier invoices due and the items running low. Trades and building Trades Quotes sent and accepted, jobs finished but not invoiced, and overdue invoices by customer. Clinic or salon Health and beauty Appointments booked for the week ahead, no-shows last week, and gaps in the diary. Shop or dairy Retail Sales against last year, best and slowest sellers, and stock below its reorder point. Adviser or accountant Professional services Client files waiting on documents, work in progress not yet billed, and fees overdue. Transport and delivery Transport Deliveries completed, proof of delivery still missing, fuel spend and kilometres travelled. For shops, a daily version of the sales summary is often worth having too. You can read more in our page on automation for shops and dairies .

docs.t: Your business numbers, every week: Skip the vanity numbers
docs.a: Some numbers feel good but rarely change what you do. Website visits, social media followers and total sales since the business opened are the usual suspects. They're not useless. But they don't belong on a one-screen weekly view unless you act on them. Watch for these traps as well: Turnover without margin. A record sales week can still lose money if it came from discounts or overtime. If you can, show gross profit alongside sales. Averages that hide problems. A healthy-looking average invoice age can hide one customer who's months behind. List the worst offenders by name instead. Numbers without an owner. Every figure on the summary should have someone who acts when it moves. If nobody would, remove it. Your accountant can help you pick the few financial measures that matter most for your type of business, and check that the summary agrees with what your accounts show. Not sure which numbers to track, or where they all live? Our free session is a good place to start. We look at your current tools and leave you with a written plan you keep. You can book a free session here .

docs.t: The Privacy Act 2020 and automation
docs.a: Automation moves personal information faster and further than a person with a spreadsheet. That's the point, but it means privacy under the Privacy Act 2020 needs a few minutes of thought before you build, not after. This is general information, not legal advice. Check anything specific with a lawyer or the Privacy Commissioner's guidance. Personal information is anything that identifies a person, and most business automations touch some. Collect only what you need, tell people why, keep it secure, and delete it when you no longer need it. Know where your data is hosted and whether any AI tool uses it for training. Privacy breaches that cause, or are likely to cause, serious harm must be reported to the Privacy Commissioner and the people affected as soon as practicable.
docs.x: The Privacy Act 2020 and automation Compliance What New Zealand businesses should check before automating anything that touches personal information.

docs.t: Does the Privacy Act 2020 apply to my small business?
docs.q: Does the Privacy Act 2020 apply to my small business?
docs.a: Generally, yes. The Act applies to businesses and organisations of all sizes in New Zealand, including sole traders, when they collect and use personal information. If you are unsure how it applies to you, check the Privacy Commissioner's guidance or talk to a lawyer.

docs.t: Can I use AI tools with customer information?
docs.q: Can I use AI tools with customer information?
docs.a: You can, but check first how the tool stores the information, where it is hosted, who can see it and whether it is used to train the provider's AI model. Many business plans offer settings that keep your data out of training, and you should confirm this in writing before sending personal information.

docs.t: Is it a problem if my data is stored overseas?
docs.q: Is it a problem if my data is stored overseas?
docs.a: Not automatically. Many cloud tools store data overseas. You stay responsible for the information, so check where it is held and how the provider protects it. The Privacy Commissioner's guidance covers sending information overseas in more detail, and choosing tools that host in New Zealand or Australia can make these questions simpler.

docs.t: What should I do if an automation sends personal information to the wrong person?
docs.q: What should I do if an automation sends personal information to the wrong person?
docs.a: Act quickly to contain it, such as asking the recipient to delete it and fixing the cause. Then assess whether it could cause serious harm. If it has or is likely to, you must notify the Privacy Commissioner and the affected people as soon as practicable. Keep a record of what happened either way.

docs.t: The Privacy Act 2020 and automation: Why the Privacy Act 2020 matters when you automate
docs.a: General information, not legal advice. This guide explains the Privacy Act 2020 in broad terms for small business owners thinking about automation. It doesn't cover every situation. For anything specific to your business, check the guidance from the Office of the Privacy Commissioner or talk to a lawyer. Picture a Friday afternoon. Your new booking reminders have been running all week and they're working beautifully. Then a customer rings: "Why did I get a text about someone else's appointment?" A person copying details between systems might make that mistake once. An automation set up wrongly can repeat it many times before anyone notices. Automation doesn't change the rules. It does change the scale. That's why a few privacy questions belong at the start of every automation project, not after. The Privacy Act 2020 is New Zealand's main privacy law. It sets out how businesses and organisations should collect, store, use and share information about people. It applies to businesses of all sizes, from a sole trader to a large company, and the Office of the Privacy Commissioner is the regulator. The Act is built around 13 information privacy principles. Together they cover the whole life of personal information: Why and how you collect it. How you store and protect it. People's right to see and correct it. How long you keep it. When you can use or share it. It also expects every organisation to have a privacy officer. In a small business that's often the owner or office manager.

docs.t: The Privacy Act 2020 and automation: What counts as personal information
docs.a: Personal information is any information about an identifiable individual. The simple test: if you can tell who it's about, it counts. In a typical small business that includes: Customer names, phone numbers, email and street addresses Booking history, purchase history and notes about preferences Health details in a clinic or salon intake form Financial details held by an adviser or accountant Staff records, rosters, timesheets and pay details Call recordings, voicemails, photos, text messages and emails Information about a business itself, such as a company's trading name or GST number, is generally not personal information. But a sole trader's details often are, because the business and the person are the same. Most automations touch at least some of this. Here's how it shows up in everyday tasks: Automation Personal information it uses Booking reminder A name and phone number Quote drafted from site notes Often the customer's address File note written from a call Possibly sensitive details None of that stops you automating. It just means you should know where the information goes.

docs.t: The Privacy Act 2020 and automation: Collect only the personal information you need, and say why
docs.a: Only collect personal information you have a real business reason for. Automation makes it tempting to capture everything because storage is cheap. Resist that. Every extra field is something you have to protect, and something that can leak. A quick test for each form field. What would break if we stopped asking for this? If the answer is nothing, take it off the form. When you collect information, people should generally know what you're collecting, why, who will see it, and how they can ask to see or correct it. A short privacy statement on your website, booking form or intake form usually covers this. Watch for new uses. Say you used to only call customers, and your new automation sends reminders by text. That's the information being used in a new way, so check that your privacy statement still covers it.

docs.t: The Privacy Act 2020 and automation: Keeping personal information secure: storage and access
docs.a: The Act expects you to keep personal information reasonably safe from loss, misuse and unauthorised access. What's reasonable depends on how sensitive it is. For most small businesses, the basics go a long way: Turn on two-factor authentication. Do it on email, accounting, booking and any tool that holds customer data. It means a password alone isn't enough to get in. Give each person their own login. Don't share one, so you can remove access when someone leaves. Limit access to what each role needs. A receptionist may need booking details but not clinical notes. Keep a list of which tools hold personal information. Note who has access to each. It's also useful when you need to answer a customer's request to see their information. Check automations that send messages. Make sure they can't send one customer's details to another. People also have a right to ask for the personal information you hold about them, and to ask for it to be corrected. If your information is spread across several tools, answering that request is hard. A well connected set of business apps with one main record per customer makes it much easier.

docs.t: The Privacy Act 2020 and automation: Where your data is hosted, and sending it overseas
docs.a: Many cloud tools store data on servers outside New Zealand. That's not automatically a problem, but you remain responsible for the information. In general terms: Storing isn't the same as handing over. Using a cloud provider to store or process information for you is different from handing it to another organisation for its own use. Either way, you remain accountable for it. Sharing overseas for their own use has extra rules. If you plan to share personal information with an organisation overseas for its own use, read the Privacy Commissioner's guidance first, because extra rules apply. Read the provider's terms. See where data is stored, who can access it and what happens to it if you leave. Choosing tools hosted in New Zealand or Australia often makes these questions simpler. How we handle it. When we build automations, client data is handled under the Privacy Act 2020, and the data we store is hosted in New Zealand or Australia. Automations are built in your own accounts, so you keep control of them and keep everything if you stop working with us. Only Ambs works on client projects and sees client data; we don't use contractors. Other tools in the chain, such as your accounting or email software, have their own hosting. So they belong on your checklist too.

docs.t: The Privacy Act 2020 and automation: AI tools and training data: what to check first
docs.a: AI tools raise one extra question: does the provider use what you send it to train its models? With some free or consumer versions, it may. With many business versions there are settings or terms that keep your data out of training. But you need to check rather than assume. Before you put customer or staff information into an AI tool, find out: Is our data used for training? Get the answer from the provider's terms or settings, not from a sales page. Where is it processed and stored? And for how long? Who at the provider can see it? And under what circumstances? Do we need to send personal details at all? Often an AI reply or summary works just as well with names and contact details removed. Who checks the output? AI can get facts wrong. Anything sent to a customer, or used to make a decision about a person, should be checked by someone. The data we handle for clients is never used to train anyone's AI model. The AI tools we use on client data run on business plans that don't train on that data. Thinking about AI for customer messages? Our guide to AI customer replies for small business covers how to keep a person in the loop.

docs.t: The Privacy Act 2020 and automation: How long to keep it: retention and deletion
docs.a: Don't keep personal information for longer than you need it for the purpose you collected it. Automation tends to keep everything forever by default, so set a rule and build it in. Balance this against other obligations. For example, businesses generally need to keep business records for seven years for tax purposes. Your accountant can tell you which records that covers. Good candidates for scheduled deletion are often: Old enquiry forms Expired leads Copies of ID that were only needed once Remember the copies. An enquiry form might be saved in your website, emailed to two inboxes and copied into a spreadsheet. Deleting one leaves three.

docs.t: The Privacy Act 2020 and automation: When something goes wrong: privacy breaches
docs.a: A privacy breach is unauthorised or accidental access to, or disclosure, change, loss or destruction of, personal information. It's often more ordinary than it sounds. An email sent to the wrong customer, a lost laptop or a hacked inbox can all be breaches. If a breach has caused, or is likely to cause, serious harm to someone, the Act requires you to notify the Privacy Commissioner and the affected people, as soon as practicable. The Privacy Commissioner's website explains how to assess harm and how to report. Plan for mistakes before they happen. Know who decides whether a breach is serious, how you'll contain it, and where you'll record what happened. A little planning now can save a stressful afternoon later.

docs.t: The Privacy Act 2020 and automation: A privacy checklist before you automate
docs.a: Run through these questions for any automation that touches personal information. Still deciding which task to start with? Our guide on choosing what to automate first can help. What personal information does this automation use, and do we need all of it? Does our privacy statement cover this use? Which tools will the information pass through, and where is each one hosted? Who will be able to see it, and is two-factor authentication on for each tool? Does any AI tool in the chain use our data for training? Could it send one person's information to someone else? How would we notice? How long will the information be kept, and in how many places? Who is responsible for this automation, and who do they call if something goes wrong? If you can answer these clearly, you're in a good position. If several are unclear, that's a sign to tidy up the process before you automate it. Come across a term you're not sure about? Our automation glossary explains them simply.

docs.t: Websites that turn visitors into calls
docs.a: A small business website has one main job: help the right people get in touch. That rarely takes clever design. It takes a short list of basics done properly, from load speed to a contact form that actually reaches you. Many visitors arrive on a phone. Design for that first and check every page on a real phone. The first screen should say what you do, where, and how to get in touch, with a tap-to-call button. Contact forms should save every enquiry somewhere safe, not just send an email that can go missing. Local search depends on a complete Google Business Profile and the same name, address and phone everywhere. Measure calls and form enquiries, not just visits, so you know what the website is doing for you.
docs.x: Websites that turn visitors into calls Digital tools What makes a small-business website earn enquiries, from speed to languages to the contact form.

docs.t: How fast should a small business website be?
docs.q: How fast should a small business website be?
docs.a: As fast as you can reasonably make it, especially on a phone with a weak signal. Free tools such as Google's PageSpeed Insights will test your pages and point out what is slowing them down, which is often large images or too many add-ons.

docs.t: Do I need my website in more than one language?
docs.q: Do I need my website in more than one language?
docs.a: Not always, but if many of your customers are more comfortable in another language, a few translated pages covering your services, prices and contact details can make it much easier for them to get in touch. Have translations checked by a fluent speaker rather than relying on automatic translation alone.

docs.t: Is it all right to put reviews on my website?
docs.q: Is it all right to put reviews on my website?
docs.a: Yes, as long as they are genuine reviews from real customers, shown as they were written, with permission where needed. Never write or buy reviews. Linking to your Google reviews is a simple, honest option.

docs.t: How do I know if my website is bringing in enquiries?
docs.q: How do I know if my website is bringing in enquiries?
docs.a: Count them. Track how many people tap your phone number and submit your contact form each week, and ask new customers how they found you. Website visits alone do not tell you much.

docs.t: Websites that turn visitors into calls: What a small business website is really for
docs.a: Picture someone standing at the bus stop with water dripping through their kitchen ceiling at home. They've searched "plumber near me" on their phone, opened your website, and now they're squinting at it, trying to find your number before the bus arrives. That's who most of your visitors are. They already have a problem they want solved: a burst pipe, a sore back, a tax return, a catering order. They want to know three things, quickly: do you do this, do you work near me, and how do I reach you? A website that answers those clearly will usually do more for you than one with beautiful pictures and a vague headline. This guide covers the basics that tend to matter most for New Zealand small businesses. You can check most of them yourself in an afternoon, with your phone in your hand.
docs.x: Websites that turn visitors into calls

docs.t: Websites that turn visitors into calls: Website speed and mobile come first
docs.a: Many visitors to a local business website arrive on a phone, often on mobile data, often while doing something else. If the page is slow or awkward, they go back to the search results and try the next business. The good news is that the usual fixes aren't complicated: Smaller images. Photos straight from a camera or phone are often far larger than a web page needs. Resizing and compressing them is often the single biggest speed gain. Fewer add-ons. Every chat widget, slider, pop-up and tracking script adds weight. Keep the ones that earn their place. Readable text without zooming. Body text should be comfortable to read on a small screen, with buttons big enough to tap with a thumb. Test on a real phone. Not just a desktop browser made narrow. Try it on mobile data, not only your office Wi-Fi. Run a free speed check. Free tools such as Google's PageSpeed Insights will test a page and list what's slowing it down. You don't need to chase a perfect score, but do fix anything it flags as a serious problem.
docs.x: Websites that turn visitors into calls

docs.t: Websites that turn visitors into calls: A first screen that gets you calls
docs.a: The first screen is what people see before they scroll. On a phone that's not much space, so it needs to work hard. Four jobs, in this order: Say what you do, in plain words. "Plumber in West Auckland, same-day callouts" beats "Excellence in every drop". Say where you work. Suburbs, city or region. People want to know you'll come to them. Give one obvious next step. A tap-to-call button, a booking button or a short form, whichever you most want people to use. Show one reason to trust you. Years in business, a licence or registration you hold, or a genuine review. Go back to the person at the bus stop. If those four things are on the first screen, they can ring you before the bus pulls in.
docs.x: Websites that turn visitors into calls

docs.t: Websites that turn visitors into calls: Tap-to-call: your phone number, one tap away
docs.a: On a phone, your number should be a link that starts a call with one tap. It sounds obvious, but many sites show the number as plain text or inside an image, which forces people to copy it by hand. Put it in the header so it's visible on every page. And make sure it goes to a phone that someone answers, or to voicemail that someone checks. If you're often on a job or with a client when the phone rings, missed calls can quietly cost you work. An automatic text back to missed callers can help: Sorry we missed your call, we're on a job right now. Reply here with what you need and we'll call you back. – Harbour Plumbing (example) Our page on automation for clinics and salons describes how missed-call follow-ups work.
docs.x: Websites that turn visitors into calls

docs.t: Websites that turn visitors into calls: Contact forms that actually reach you
docs.a: A contact form that quietly fails is worse than no form at all. The customer thinks they've been in touch, and you never hear from them. Forms fail more often than people expect. Emails land in spam, a mailbox is full, the staff member who received them has left, or a website update breaks the sending. Test your form today. Fill it in as a customer would, from your phone, and check it arrives. Then do it again once a month. It only takes a moment, and it costs nothing. A sturdier set-up saves every enquiry somewhere first, then sends the notification: Saved, not just emailed. Each enquiry is stored in a spreadsheet, CRM (customer relationship management system) or your job app, so nothing is lost if an email goes astray. A copy to the customer. A short automatic reply confirming you received it and when they can expect to hear back. Only the fields you need. Name, a way to reply and what they need. Every extra field puts some people off, and it's more personal information to look after. A clear thank-you message on screen, plus a phone number in case they'd rather call. Here's what that automatic reply might look like from the customer's side: Hi, my kitchen tap is leaking under the sink. Can someone come out this week? Mere, Henderson Thanks Mere, we've got your message. We'll be in touch by the end of the next working day. If it's urgent, give us a call. Once enquiries are saved in one place, they can flow straight into your other tools. Our guide to AI customer replies for small business covers how common questions can be answered quickly while a person still handles the rest.
docs.x: Websites that turn visitors into calls

docs.t: Websites that turn visitors into calls: Pages in your customers' languages
docs.a: New Zealand's communities speak many languages, and plenty of people feel more confident booking a service or asking about prices in their first language. If a good share of your customers speak, for example, Chinese, Hindi, Punjabi, Samoan, Tongan or te reo Māori, translated pages can make it much easier for them to get in touch. You don't need to translate the whole site at once. Start with the pages that lead to an enquiry: your services, prices or how pricing works, opening hours and contact details. A few tips: Have translations checked by a fluent speaker. Automatic translation is a useful first draft, not a finished page. Let people switch language easily from every page, and remember their choice. If you offer a service in another language, say so clearly, and make sure someone can actually reply in it. Our own website is available in English, Chinese, Hindi, te reo Māori and Punjabi for exactly this reason, and we speak with customers in English, Hindi and Punjabi.

docs.t: Websites that turn visitors into calls: Getting found on Google: local SEO basics
docs.a: SEO (search engine optimisation) is the work of helping search engines understand your website so it appears when people search. For a local business, most of the value comes from a few basics. What to do Why it helps Complete your Google Business Profile This is the free listing that can appear in Google Maps and local results. Fill in your category, service area, hours, photos and a link to your website, and keep it up to date. Use the same name, address and phone everywhere Your website, Google Business Profile, social media pages and directory listings should match exactly, so search engines are confident they all describe the same business. Write a clear title and description for each page The page title and description are often what show in search results. Put the service and place first, such as "Electrician in Hamilton". Give each main service its own page A useful page about each service, with real details, prices or how pricing works, and the areas you cover, matches what people actually search for. Answer common questions The questions customers ask you on the phone are often the questions they type into Google. No quick magic. Local SEO tends to build over months. Be wary of anyone who promises first place on Google.
docs.x: Websites that turn visitors into calls

docs.t: Websites that turn visitors into calls: Trust signals, without fake reviews
docs.a: People want some reassurance before they call a business they've never used. Honest trust signals include: Your real name and a photo of you or your team Where you're based and the areas you cover Licences, registrations or memberships you genuinely hold Photos of your actual work, with the customer's permission Genuine reviews, shown as written, or a link to your Google reviews Clear information on how pricing works, even if it's "free quote after a site visit" Never fake it. Don't write, buy or edit reviews, and don't show badges or awards you haven't earned. Apart from the ethical problem, misleading claims can breach consumer law and search engine policies, and customers often spot them.
docs.x: Websites that turn visitors into calls

docs.t: Websites that turn visitors into calls: Accessibility: a website everyone can use
docs.a: An accessible website works for people with low vision, colour blindness or shaky hands, and for people who use a screen reader. It also tends to work better for everyone else. The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) are the usual reference, but you can start with the basics: Strong contrast between text and background Text that can be enlarged without breaking the layout Descriptive alt text on meaningful images, so screen readers can describe them Buttons and links that say what they do, rather than "click here" Forms with clear labels and error messages that explain what to fix

docs.t: Websites that turn visitors into calls: Count the calls, not just the visits
docs.a: Visits and page views are easy to count, but they don't pay the bills. What you really want to know is how many people got in touch. Track: Taps on your phone number Contact form enquiries received and saved Bookings made through the website How new customers say they found you, asked on the first call Put these on your weekly summary next to sales and jobs, and you can start to see whether website changes are making a difference. Our guide to your business numbers every week explains how to set that up. If you'd like a website built around these basics, see our websites, portals and dashboards service .

docs.t: Automation glossary
docs.a: API, webhook, LLM, CRM. Automation and AI come with a lot of jargon. Here are the terms you're most likely to hear, explained in plain words, with a note on why each one matters to a small business. You don't need to know these terms to automate, but they help you ask better questions. Most automations come down to a trigger, some steps and an action, joined up by an API or webhook. AI tools can draft and summarise, but a person should check anything that matters. Security and privacy terms, such as two-factor authentication and personal information, are worth knowing well.
docs.x: Automation glossary Getting started Plain-English meanings of the automation and AI terms you will hear.

docs.t: What is the difference between automation and AI?
docs.q: What is the difference between automation and AI?
docs.a: Automation follows set rules: when this happens, do that. AI can handle less predictable work, such as reading an email and drafting a reply. Many useful systems combine the two, with plain automation doing most of the work and AI helping at one or two steps.

docs.t: Do I need to understand APIs to automate my business?
docs.q: Do I need to understand APIs to automate my business?
docs.a: No. It helps to know that an API is how two programs exchange information, because it explains why some tools connect easily and others don't. The person building your automation should handle the technical detail and explain it in plain words.

docs.t: Is a chatbot the same as an AI agent?
docs.q: Is a chatbot the same as an AI agent?
docs.a: Not quite. A chatbot answers messages in a conversation. An AI agent can also take actions, such as checking a calendar and making a booking. Both should have clear limits and a way to hand over to a person.

docs.t: Automation glossary: How to use this automation glossary
docs.a: Picture a meeting about your new booking system. Someone says the API pushes a webhook to the CRM, and everyone nods. You nod too. Inside, you're wondering what any of it means, and whether it's going to cost you. You're not alone. Tech people speak in shorthand, and most of it describes simple ideas. This page turns that shorthand back into plain words. Terms are listed alphabetically and grouped by letter. Each one starts with a short, simple meaning. Where it helps, there's an example from a typical New Zealand small business. Heard a term that isn't here? Ask whoever's building your system to explain it. A good builder will happily do that without making you feel silly. And where an entry touches on law or tax, it's general information, not legal or tax advice. The three words that explain most automations. A trigger starts it, a workflow sets out the steps, and an integration lets your apps pass information along the way.

docs.t: Automation glossary: A–B: AI agents, APIs and automation
docs.a: AI agent An AI system that can carry out tasks, not just answer questions. For example, it might read a booking request, check the calendar and offer a time. It should work within clear limits, with a person able to step in. API Short for application programming interface. Think of it as a secure doorway that lets one program ask another for information, or send it some. Most modern business software has one, including Xero, Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace. It's what makes most app connections possible. Approval step A point where an automation pauses so a person can check and confirm before it carries on. For example, a drafted quote waits for your OK before it goes to the customer. Automation Getting software to do a repetitive task a person used to do by hand, following the same rules every time. For example, sending booking reminders, or turning an approved job into an invoice. Not sure where to begin? Our guide on choosing what to automate first covers where to start. Backup A separate copy of your data that you can restore if the original is lost, deleted or damaged. A good backup is stored somewhere different from the original. It's also tested now and then, so you know it actually works. Bank feed A connection that brings your bank transactions into your accounting software automatically, so nobody has to type them in. It's usually the starting point for matching payments to invoices. For example, a customer's payment lands in the feed, ready to match to the invoice it pays.

docs.t: Automation glossary: C: chatbots, cloud software and CRM
docs.a: Chatbot A program that answers messages in a chat window, such as one on your website. Simple chatbots follow fixed scripts. AI chatbots can understand questions written in everyday language. Either way, there should be an easy route to a real person. Cloud software Software you use through a web browser or app, with your data stored on the provider's servers rather than on your own computer. Xero, Gmail and Google Sheets are all cloud software. For example, you can check an invoice from the café counter or the ute, not just the office PC. CRM Short for customer relationship management. It's a system that keeps all your customer details, enquiries, notes and history in one place. There's plenty of dedicated CRM software. For a very small business, though, a well organised spreadsheet in Excel or Google Sheets can do the job. CSV file A simple text file of data in rows and columns, separated by commas. Most software can export and import CSV files. That makes them a handy go-between when two tools can't connect directly. For example, you might export a customer list from one system and import it into another.

docs.t: Automation glossary: D–G: dashboards, data mapping and GST
docs.a: Dashboard A single screen that shows your key numbers, such as sales, unpaid invoices and jobs, and updates itself as things change. Our guide to your business numbers every week explains what to put on one. Data mapping Working out which piece of information in one app matches which piece in another. For example, deciding that "Client name" in your booking system goes into "Contact" in your accounting software. Getting this right is a big part of any integration. Field One piece of information in a form or record, such as a name, phone number or invoice date. Automations move information field by field. Google Business Profile Google's free listing for your business, which can appear in Google Maps and local search results. It shows your hours, location, phone number, photos and reviews. It's one of the most useful things a local business can keep up to date. For example, a public holiday change to your hours belongs here first. GST Goods and Services Tax, New Zealand's 15% tax on most goods and services. Any automation that creates quotes or invoices needs to handle GST correctly. Your accountant can confirm how it applies to your business.

docs.t: Automation glossary: H–N: hallucinations, integrations and no-code
docs.a: Hallucination When an AI tool states something that sounds confident but is wrong or made up. It's the main reason a person should check AI-written content before it goes to a customer. For example, a drafted reply might quote opening hours you don't actually keep. Hosting Where a website, app or data actually lives: the servers that store it and keep it running. Hosting location matters for speed and for privacy. Data we store for clients is hosted in New Zealand or Australia. Human in the loop A design where a person reviews or approves key steps of an automated process, rather than letting it run entirely on its own. It's sensible wherever a mistake would be costly or embarrassing. Integration A connection between two pieces of software so they share information automatically. For example, an integration might turn each approved quote into a draft invoice in Xero. Our guide to connecting your business apps covers how they work. LLM Short for large language model. It's the type of AI behind most modern chat and writing tools. It has learned patterns from a huge amount of text. That lets it understand questions and write replies, summaries and drafts. Low-code Tools that let you build apps or automations mostly by dragging and configuring, with a little code where needed. They sit between no-code tools and fully custom software. Multi-factor authentication The general name for logins that need more than one proof of identity. Two-factor authentication is the most common kind. No-code Tools that let people build automations, forms or simple apps without writing any code, usually by choosing steps from menus. They're great for simple jobs. Complex processes can outgrow them, though. Notifiable privacy breach A privacy breach that has caused, or is likely to cause, serious harm to someone. Under the Privacy Act 2020, you must tell the Privacy Commissioner and the people affected as soon as practicable.

docs.t: Automation glossary: O–S: OCR, the Privacy Act and SEO
docs.a: OCR Short for optical character recognition. It's software that reads text from a photo or scanned document and turns it into data a computer can use. Receipt and bill capture tools use it to pull details from documents. For example, snap a supplier invoice and the amount and date come out ready to use. Permissions Settings that control who can see or change what in a system. Good permissions mean each person sees only what their role needs. For example, your casual staff can see the roster, but not the bank account. Personal information Any information about an identifiable person, such as a name, phone number, address, health details or booking history. The Privacy Act 2020 sets the rules for collecting, storing and using it. Portal A private website or app where staff or customers log in to see and do things. For example, they might track a job, upload photos, approve a quote or download an invoice. It's your own app on every phone, without an app store. Privacy Act 2020 New Zealand's main privacy law. It's built around 13 information privacy principles. They cover how personal information is collected, stored, used, shared and deleted. Our guide to the Privacy Act and automation explains what to check. Prompt The instructions or question you give an AI tool. Clear prompts, with examples and limits, usually get more reliable results. For example, "Reply in two sentences, and never offer a discount" works better than "Write a reply". Scheduled task An automation that runs at a set time, rather than in response to an event. For example, a sales summary sent every Monday at 7am is a scheduled task. SEO Short for search engine optimisation. It's the work of helping search engines understand your website, so it shows up when people search for what you offer. For local businesses, it starts with clear pages and a complete Google Business Profile. Single source of truth One agreed place where a piece of information is kept and updated, with every other system reading from it. For example, if customer details live only in your CRM and flow out from there, you avoid three slightly different versions. SSL and HTTPS The security that encrypts information travelling between a website and a visitor's browser. A site using it has an address starting with https://, and browsers warn visitors when a site doesn't use it. Every website with a contact form should have it. Sync Short for synchronise. It means keeping the same information up to date in two or more places, so a change in one shows up in the others. For example, a customer's new phone number, updated once, appears everywhere it's used. Privacy terms are worth knowing well. Personal information, permissions and notifiable breaches aren't just tech talk. They're where the Privacy Act 2020 meets your everyday systems, so it pays to understand them before you automate anything that holds customer details.

docs.t: Automation glossary: T–Z: triggers, webhooks and workflows
docs.a: Template A reusable layout for a document or message, with gaps the automation fills in. For example, the customer's name and appointment time in a reminder text. Training data The information used to teach an AI model. Some AI providers use what customers send them to train future models, so check the settings and terms before sharing business data. Data we handle for clients is never used to train anyone's AI model. The AI tools we use on client data run on business plans that don't train on it. Trigger The event that starts an automation. A new booking, an email arriving, a form being submitted or a job being marked complete are all common triggers. Two-factor authentication A login that needs your password plus a second check, usually a code from your phone or an authenticator app. It makes it much harder for someone with a stolen password to get in. It's worth turning on for email, accounting and banking. Webhook A message one app sends to another the moment something happens, such as "a new order has just come in". It lets automations react straight away, rather than checking for changes every few minutes. For example, an online order can reach your packing list within moments. Workflow The series of steps a task goes through from start to finish, whether done by people, software or both. Writing the workflow down is usually the first step in automating it. For example: enquiry comes in, quote goes out, job is booked, invoice is sent.
